title: WAYGO — Agent-Native Travel Marketplace for Africa
pitch: AI agents discover, verify and compare African travel packages while travellers retain control of contact, booking and payment.
about_excerpt: AI agents discover, verify and compare African travel packages while travellers retain control of contact, booking and payment. Like 1 Comment Story Updates WAYGO's WebMCP agent searches, verifies and compares Umrah packages, then pauses for human approval before agency contact or payment. Inspiration Across Africa, travel packages are often fragmented across WhatsApp messages, social media posts and disconnected agency websites. Travellers may need to compare incomplete offers manually while also determining whether an agency is trustworthy. Important details—such as flights, accommodation quality, visa support, transfers and cancellation terms—are rarely presented consistently. This inspired me to build WAYGO , an agent-native travel marketplace based on a simple question: How can a traveller delegate difficult travel research to an AI agent without surrendering control of consequential decisions? I did not want to create another generic AI itinerary chatbot. I wanted the website and the agent to work together. The agent should handle repetitive discovery, verification and comparison tasks, while the traveller remains inside a visual marketplace where every action can be reviewed and changed. What it does WAYGO allows travellers to search and compare representative African travel packages manually or ask a compatible browser agent to complete the research through WebMCP. For example, a traveller can ask: I want to perform Umrah from Abuja in October with a budget of ₦2.5 million. Find suitable packages, verify the best agency, compare the strongest two options and shortlist them. Prepare agency contact, but do not book or pay. The agent discovers WAYGO’s structured tools, executes the workflow and updates the same interface the traveller is viewing. Search filters change, packages are selected for comparison, the shortlist count updates and verification evidence is returned. WAYGO exposes five WebMCP tools: search_travel_packages filters packages by origin, budget and trip type. verify_agency returns the available verification evidence for an agency. compare_packages selects up to three packages for comparison. create_shortlist updates the traveller’s visible shortlist. request_agency_contact prepares a contact request but stops for human approval. The final tool deliberately returns human_approval_required . It opens an approval dialog explaining what would be shared and confirms that no booking or payment will be made. How I built it I built WAYGO with React, TypeScript, Vinext, Tailwind CSS, WebMCP and Cloudflare Workers . The challenge prototype contains representative Nigerian Umrah packages with different departure cities, prices, accommodation levels, durations and inclusions. Its current verification evidence is simulated demonstration data rather than live regulatory information. I registered the tools in the top-level page using document.modelContext.registerTool() . Each tool has: A clear name and description A constrained JSON input schema An execution function connected to the application’s React state A structured result that the agent can interpret My most important architectural decision was connecting the WebMCP tools to the same state used by the visual marketplace. The agent is not operating an invisible parallel system. When it searches, compares or shortlists packages, the traveller sees those changes immediately. I also designed WAYGO as a progressive enhancement. When WebMCP is unavailable, the website remains functional through its manual filters, package cards, comparison controls and approval dialog. Challenges I ran into Designing tools around user intentions It would have been easy to expose low-level actions such as “click this button” or “change this field.” Instead, I designed tools around meaningful travel intentions: search, verify, compare, shortlist and prepare contact. This required carefully defining each tool’s responsibility and structured response. Maintaining a shared human-agent workspace The agent’s actions needed to remain visible and understandable. I connected tool execution directly to the marketplace state so users can inspect and modify every result. This makes WAYGO a cooperative workspace rather than a chatbot beside a disconnected website. Establishing a safe autonomy boundary Travel transactions can involve personal information and substantial financial commitments. I prevented the agent from booking or paying. Even the contact workflow stops at a clear approval dialog. The agent prepares the next step, but the human decides whether it should happen. Working with an experimental standard WebMCP is still experimental and is not available in every browser or model configuration. I tested WAYGO in a compatible ChatGPT integrated browser and confirmed that all five tools were discoverable and functional. I retained complete manual controls so the marketplace remains usable in ordinary browsers. Keeping the prototype focused A production marketplace would require live inventory, licensed-agency integrations, evidence-backed verification, identity management and payment infrastructure. For this challenge, I focused on one polished workflow: Search → Verify → Compare → Shortlist → Human approval → Contact preparation Accomplishments I’m proud of Built and deployed a functioning agent-native travel marketplace. Implemented five discoverable WebMCP tools. Synchronized agent actions with the visible human interface. Demonstrated structured agency-verification evidence. Created a budget-aware search, comparison and shortlist workflow. Established a clear human-approval boundary before agency contact. Prevented autonomous booking and payment. Made the application responsive and manually usable without WebMCP. Published the complete source code and implementation documentation. What I learned The biggest lesson I learned was that making a website agent-native involves much more than adding a chatbot. Good agent tools need to represent genuine user goals, use predictable schemas and return structured results. Agent actions should remain visible in the human interface so users understand what changed and why. I also learned that autonomy should be designed in layers. Search and comparison are relatively low-risk tasks that can be delegated confidently. Contact, booking and payment require progressively stronger human confirmation. WebMCP makes it possible to express these boundaries while keeping the agent useful. Most importantly, building WAYGO showed me how agent-native interfaces can address problems that are especially relevant in African markets: fragmented information, inconsistent digital experiences and the need for stronger trust signals. What’s next for WAYGO My next step is to connect WAYGO to licensed Nigerian and African travel agencies, ingest live package availability, verify licences against authoritative sources and support additional departure cities and travel categories. I also plan to add consent-based agency messaging and persistent traveller shortlists. Booking and payment would remain separately confirmed actions. My long-term goal is to make WAYGO trusted infrastructure for human-agent travel collaboration across Africa: agents handle fragmented research, the marketplace provides transparent shared state and people remain in control where it matters.
